newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian far-right sees a sell-out to foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Austrian far-right sees a sell-out to foreigners.

text.p: Austrian far right leader Joerg Haider, snapping at the government's heels ahead of European and Vienna polls, accused the ruling coalition on Saturday of pandering to foreigners at the expense of ordinary Austrians.

The nation will vote for the first time in European parliamentary elections on October 13. A Vienna state poll on the same day looks certain to end half a century of Social Democrat rule in the capital.

"I am on the people's side, unlike the government. They made a mess of negotiating Austria's entry into the European Union and now we are having to pay for it," Haider told a cheering crowd in the working class Vienna district of Favoriten.

Around 1,000 people, many of them elderly, gathered in torrential rain to hear the populist opposition leader renew his call for lower contributions to Brussels and more money for pensioners, workers and their families.
"Jobs have gone in the textile industry and the food industry thanks to the EU. The government promised that membership would create 38,000 new jobs but in fact we have lost 40,000," Haider said.
Recent voter surveys show Haider's Freedom Party has the backing of a quarter of Austrians -- only a few percentage points behind junior coalition partner the People's Party.
Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats have 31 percent support -- almost a post-World War Two low.
Haider insisted the Freedom Party alone would further Austrian interests in the European Parliament and fight to prevent the national currency's dilution by "weak" southern European currencies.

"If the drachma rubs up against the strong schilling, obviously the schilling will be weakened and your savings will be worth less," he told the crowd, renewing his call for a referendum on a single European currency.
"Austrians must decide whether they want a single European currency, not Brussels."
Haider, whose anti-immigration policies have struck a chord with voters worried about rising unemployment and a perceived increase in crime, called for an end to the influx of foreigners.
"The government's so-called integration policy is a disaster. They are ready to open the doors to another 153,000 foreigners who will take school places, training places and flats," Haider said.
Turkish youths were demanding protection money on the capital's streets, he claimed. "This is our city. It is not Istanbul."
The Freedom Party ran into controversy last month after billboards bearing the slogan "Vienna must not become Chicago" appeared across the capital.
An unrepentant Haider delivered his speech on Saturday from a stage decorated with the offending posters.

Down the street a Social Democrat stage attracted little attention from passers-by. Haider claimed Vienna mayor Michael Haeupl had cancelled a scheduled appearance because of a lack of voter interest.
